> **What this case shows** — healthy walking presses the ground in a double-humped pattern (a loading peak,
> a mid-stance dip as the body vaults over the leg, a push-off peak). Impaired gait flattens it. This case
> certifies that as a group difference across 707 real gait trials. Each trial's vertical-GRF *dynamic
> range* (loading peak − mid-stance trough) comes from the **certified** `grfLandmarks`; the **certified**
> `twoSampleTTest` compares healthy controls (n=208) and knee-pathology patients (n=499), reproducing
> **`scipy.stats.ttest_ind`** *and* base R **`t.test`** **bit-for-bit**. Controls have **~1.87x** the
> dynamic range (0.37 vs 0.20 BW, t=17.3, p~3e-48).

::: {.callout-tip title="The recipe you'll learn"}
**Workflow** — `grfLandmarks()` per trial → dynamic range → `twoSampleTTest()` between groups.
**Way of thinking** — turn a waveform into one interpretable number, then test it. The GRF double-hump's
depth (dynamic range) captures how dynamically a person loads the limb; a flattened hump is the mark of
cautious, impaired gait, and the group test makes the observation inferential.
**Ecosystem usage** — `PhysioMoCap::grfLandmarks()`, `PhysioAnalysis::twoSampleTTest()`.
:::

## Proposition

Healthy controls (n=208) have a larger vertical-GRF dynamic range than knee-pathology patients (n=499) --
mean 0.367 vs 0.196 BW, ratio ~1.87, Welch t=17.3 on 337 df, p~2.8e-48; `twoSampleTTest` reproduces
`scipy.stats.ttest_ind(equal_var=FALSE)` and base R `t.test` bit-for-bit.

## Question & goal

**The question is a pathology signature and a chained certification: is the flattened-GRF pattern of
impaired gait a significant group difference, and does the two-sample test reproduce the reference on a
large cohort?** The goal is to turn the sibling case's descriptive landmarks into a certified inferential
result.

## Challenge & approach

For each trial we take the body-weight- and time-normalised vertical GRF, extract the loading peak and
mid-stance trough with `grfLandmarks` (certified in the
[gait-grf-gaitrec](../gait-grf-gaitrec/index.qmd) case), form the dynamic range (peak − trough), and
compare controls with patients using `twoSampleTTest`, checking t and p against `scipy.stats.ttest_ind`
and base R.

```
GaitRec vGRF: control (n=208) & patient (n=499) → grfLandmarks → dynamic range = peak1 - trough
  control mean 0.367 BW   ·   patient mean 0.196 BW   ·   ratio 1.87
  twoSampleTTest (Welch) → t = 17.3, df = 337, p ~ 2.8e-48   vs scipy & base R → |diff| = 0
```

## Data

**GaitRec (Horsak et al. 2020)**: processed vertical GRF (body-weight- and time-normalised), healthy
controls (n=208 trials) vs knee-pathology patients (n=499 trials), shod, standardised speed. Details in
[`artifacts/data_sources.json`](artifacts/data_sources.json).

## Results

![Left: the mean vertical GRF over stance — the control double-hump (blue) is pronounced (loading and push-off peaks ~1.1 BW, a deep mid-stance trough ~0.75), while the patient curve (red) is flattened (lower peaks, a raised trough ~0.83). Right: the per-trial dynamic range (peak − trough) by group — control 0.37 vs patient 0.20 BW, a ~1.87x difference (t=17.3, p~3e-48).](artifacts/figure.png)

*How to read this:* left — the flattening is the whole story: less dynamic loading, less mid-stance
unloading, weaker push-off. Right — that flattening reduces the dynamic range by nearly half, cleanly
separating the groups.

| Quantity | Value |
|---|--:|
| control / patient mean dynamic range | 0.37 / 0.20 BW |
| **control / patient ratio** | **~1.87** |
| **Welch t** (df 337) | **17.3** |
| −log₁₀ p | 47.6 (p ~ 2.8e-48) |
| n control / patient | 208 / 499 |
| vs `scipy.stats.ttest_ind` / base R (\|diff\|) | **0** (bit-for-bit) |

The two-sample test equals both references exactly, and the flattening is a very large, significant effect.
Values trace to [`artifacts/grf_summary.csv`](artifacts/grf_summary.csv).

## Conclusion

`twoSampleTTest`, certified in the balance cohort, reproduces the reference here too, on the certified
`grfLandmarks`. The transferable takeaway: **the depth of the GRF double-hump is a compact, mechanistic
read-out of gait quality — it nearly halves in knee pathology. Reducing a waveform to a certified landmark
feature and testing it between groups turns a qualitative "flattened GRF" impression into a quantified,
reproducible, statistically-certified difference.**

## Open questions

- This pools the knee-pathology class vs controls with one processed vGRF per trial; GaitRec spans several
  pathology classes and sessions, supporting per-class effect sizes and a classifier, and the dynamic
  range is one of several GRF features (peaks, impulses, loading rates). The double-hump dynamic range is
  the single most interpretable summary of the flattening. *Documented, not escalated.*

## Using this in your own analysis

| Step | Function | Package |
|---|---|---|
| GRF landmarks (peaks, trough) | `grfLandmarks()` | PhysioMoCap |
| Two-sample (Welch) t-test | `twoSampleTTest()` | PhysioAnalysis |

**Reading the result.**

- **dynamic range** — the double-hump depth in BW; larger = more dynamic loading. A flattened GRF (small
  range) signals cautious or impaired gait.
- **effect size** — report the group means and ratio with the p-value; here the ~1.87x separation on a
  707-trial cohort is both large and overwhelmingly significant.

**The recipe, copy-runnable:**

```r
library(PhysioMoCap); library(PhysioAnalysis)

dr <- function(M) apply(M, 1, function(v) { lm <- grfLandmarks(v); lm[1] - lm[2] })  # peak1 - trough
twoSampleTTest(dr(control_vGRF), dr(patient_vGRF))   # Welch t, p, df -- bit-for-bit vs scipy/base R
```

**Auditing the numbers.** Every value on this page traces to
[`artifacts/grf_summary.csv`](artifacts/grf_summary.csv), and [`audit.py`](audit.py) re-checks the Welch t,
p and df, the bit-exact match against scipy and base R, the control > patient direction and ratio, and the
honestly noted scope (reuses the certified twoSampleTTest; dynamic range from the certified grfLandmarks;
cross-sectional association).
